items.title: 2026 Volvo EX30 Pros and Cons Review: Fewer Buttons, More Bugs
items.summary:
You’d think clean design breeds good UX, but that’s not always the case. Soon after climbing into the 2026 Volvo EX30 Single Motor Plus and needing to grab the window sticker from the glovebox, I realized there was no latch in sight. I nearly gave up until I spotted it: a button on the big center touchscreen that said “glovebox.” It opened, but only after three taps. I knew I was in for a long week.

The frustrating part is that the EX30 is a good car to drive. It’s a handsome, comfortable little electric crossover with 268 horsepower, a 261-mile EPA range, and a $40,745 sticker price as tested, and I liked almost everything about it. It’s the bits around the driving experience that fall short. I once heard that UX that needs directions is bad UX, and by the end of the week I wanted directions for the mirrors, the windows, and the key card.

Here’s what the EX30 gets right and where it loses the plot.

Cy Soliman 

Pros 

It’s a clean-looking car. The exterior is streamlined, and the interior stays uncluttered because there’s almost nothing on the dash except the screen (at the cost of buttons). 

It drives smoothly, and there’s plenty of power. The single motor makes 268 hp and 253 lb-ft of torque, and it delivers it instantly, EV-style. 

The seats and ride are comfortable. Nothing about the EX30 beats you up, and it never felt like a penalty for going small. 

The size is right. It’s a compact crossover with adequate seat space and a trunk that handled everything I threw at it. It can park anywhere. 

The range was sufficient for me. The EPA rates it at 261 miles, and I…
items.t: 2026 Volvo EX30 Pros and Cons Review: Fewer Buttons, More Bugs

items.title: Toyota Honors Woman Who Put 420,000 Hard Miles on Her 1990 MR2
items.summary:
Toyotas are renowned the world over for their reliability, but that reputation shouldn’t just belong to tattered Camrys that look prepared to outlast Armageddon alongside the cockroaches. No, there are decidedly more interesting vehicles that also deserve such praise, and the automaker’s German arm recently honored some in a gathering for owners of high-mileage Toyotas. One was an MR2 that is apparently still used to haul firewood.

Claudia Noder bought her MR2 new way back in 1990. In the 36 years since, she has traveled about 420,000 miles in the mid-engine sports car. For much of that time, she commuted about 77 miles daily in it.

“My MR2 never let me down and always brought me home. And still with the first engine,” Claudia said in Toyota’s blog , translated. The owner put 3,600 miles on it just earlier this year, vacationing in the Balkans. When it gets cold, she loads up the little cargo space behind the engine with wood.

At bottom, Georg Hessmann poses with his 1987 Land Cruiser. Toyota 

Claudia was far from the only owner who received a certificate at the event. There were 96 honorees in total, all of which with at least 200,000 kilometers, or 125,000 miles, logged. Shoutout to Georg Hessmann, whose 1987 Land Cruiser has traveled 335,000 miles.

Georg says he’s driven a combined 1 million kilometers in Land Cruisers over the years, taking trips to the Western Alps and off-road parks. He’s passed the love onto his son, who owns an HZJ73 Land Cruiser of his own, with even more kilometers on the clock.

Those Land Cruisers may have lived their lives in a way a bit…
items.t: Toyota Honors Woman Who Put 420,000 Hard Miles on Her 1990 MR2

items.title: Someone Chucked a Porsche Panamera Off a Cliff and Disappeared
items.summary:
Are you missing a Porsche Panamera ? If so, could this German sports sedan found on Mulholland Drive in Studio City be it? According to CBS News, the LA Fire Department found it Saturday night, but unlike most cars that end up at the bottom of a cliff for one reason or another, its driver (or any occupants) was missing. Mmmm…

According to the report, the car was found in steep terrain, about 100 feet down a hill, with its lights on, but no one was nearby. It wasn’t outlined whether the interior of the car showed any signs of injuries or worse, but the report claims that responders looked closely in the surrounding area for any signs of life, and no one was found.

The video below by ABC7 shows the condition in which the car was found.

Whether you’re a local or a tourist, you probably know that Mulholland Drive—or a large section of it—offers one of the best roads in the country, and it’s often frequented by responsible enthusiasts and street racers alike. Could this be a case where someone simply overcooked a turn and went down the hill? Very likely. Could this be a stolen Panamera that was dumped at the end of a joyride? Totally.

It’s Thursday at noon. Do you know where your Panamera is?

Got a tip? Email us at tips@thedrive.com

items.t: Someone Chucked a Porsche Panamera Off a Cliff and Disappeared

items.title: Hollywood Car Movies Are Lame. Watch This Dirt Racing Documentary Instead
items.summary:
Racing movies are having a moment. Formula 1 got a feature film starring Brad Pitt shot during actual races, and Days of Thunder will soon get a belated sequel . Drive to Survive has also shown that real-life racing can produce enough drama to sustain a Netflix reality show. But there’s plenty more of that to be had, and it can be found far away from the glamorous settings of F1 or corporatism of NASCAR .

King of the Mountain is a new short documentary that highlights the Best Plumber 604 Racing Series, a late-model dirt series that represents the traditional grassroots of American motorsports. Directed and edited by Jeremy Frost, who produces content for the series, it focuses on the 2026 season finale held on October 17 at Thunder Mountain Speedway in Corbin, Kentucky, hence the title.

Frost Studios/King of the Mountain 

The documentary focuses on three drivers competing not only for glory, but for a $25,000 payday. In addition to the $15,000 championship purse, a $10,000 purse for winning the last feature race of the season was on offer. Skylar Mardar is the reigning series champion, and Addison Cardwell and William Blankenship were looking to unseat him. Based on the trailer, we can expect the typical cameras-shadowing-drivers format but with a less-polished aesthetic than Drive to Survive and other documentaries covering big-money professional racing.

“We wanted the film to feel as unpredictable and chaotic as the night itself,” Frost said in a statement. “That meant embracing different camera formats, handheld footage, rough edges, and the moments you wouldn’t…
items.t: Hollywood Car Movies Are Lame. Watch This Dirt Racing Documentary Instead

items.title: 2026 Audi RS6 Avant Performance Review: The Car I’m Thankful for
items.summary:
Those who have followed my career here, there, and everywhere know that I grew up with several Audis in my family. From icons like the D2 A8 and V8 quattro to the C5 A6, the one Audi I’ve always loved is the one we didn’t get in America: the RS6 Avant. A friend of mine built a C6 S6 Avant, but the RS6 has always been forbidden fruit. Then, Audi woke up one day, took its shot, and brought the C8 RS6 Avant to the U.S. as a 2001 model. The only other time the RS6 came to our shores was the C5 generation in the early 2000s, and then it was imported only as a sedan.

Up until recently, I had never driven one, and after spending a week with the 2026 Audi RS6 Avant Performance , I learned what one of my heroes is really like in real life. Unsurprisingly, it’s fantastic, and I want one. You should too.

Joel Feder 

Look at it, it’s gorgeous. With RS7 headlights slotted into the front end, gaping intakes, flared fenders, and huge rolling stock barely covering massive brakes, the RS6 Avant looks like it’s designed to go fast. Better yet, my tester rolled on 22-inch Y-spoke wheels that were forged, milled, and diamond-cut to look like a cartoon. Trademark dual exhaust outlets bookend the rear bumper in an oval shape. The entire thing looks like a muscle car shoved into a suit. No Hellcat looks this polished, and the current BMW M5 Wagon wishes it looked this good.

Joel Feder 

Inside, the RS6 Avant takes the solidly built A6 and swaps in sport bucket seats with quilted leather. My tester featured carbon twill inlays for the trim and a Cognac brown interior with granite gray…
items.t: 2026 Audi RS6 Avant Performance Review: The Car I’m Thankful for

items.title: This 3K-Mile 1968 Pontiac Le Mans Stored for 50 Years Could Be the Black Friday Deal for You
items.summary:
Are you in the market for a not-so-gently used 1968 Pontiac Le Mans survivor? If so, this may be just the machine for you. The Le Mans may not be one of the era’s most beloved big two-doors (nor does it have an iconic movie monologue dedicated to it), but nevertheless, minty examples can fetch a reasonable amount of money on the open market. And it’s not too often you see one that’s been stored in a garage for 50 years with 3,055 miles on the clock pop up on Craigslist.

To be clear, despite the listing’s claim that it fires right up, this is no time capsule. In fact, those 3,000 miles might be post-odometer-rollover. Be prepared to do some work. But at just $8,500, it’s also significantly cheaper than anything you’ll find on a popular auction site. You are looking at a relatively complete car with apparently very little rust that we think deserves a second chance. 

Considering that it has been parked in Brooklyn for what appears to be quite a long time, that corrosion claim is worthy of some follow-up. From what we can see of the body, it may well hold up, but any northeast car is gamble, let alone one that has moved very little—and we do mean very little—over the course of its lifetime. According to the listing, the car has been garaged for a half century, with a photo of its most recent proof of insurance from 1977 as evidence.

Not only do you get a running 350, but the car also has power steering and a power top. It’s pretty safe to assume that just about anything made from plastic or rubber on (or under the hood of) this car is toast. Even a garage didn’t prevent…
items.t: This 3K-Mile 1968 Pontiac Le Mans Stored for 50 Years Could Be the Black Friday Deal for You

items.title: Spy Shots Catch Mercedes Prototype Driving Around with No Body Like a Production Death Kart
items.summary:
For years, we’ve been told that EVs would fundamentally change the way we think about automotive body engineering, giving us access to a true “skateboard” chassis that could underpin virtually anything from a sports car to a semi truck. It appears that Mercedes has come up with the best possible application of this technology in the current EV era : this kick-ass, all-electric death kart… thing. 

Certainly this open chassis is serving as a testbed for something more substantial than what we can see here, but if you ask us, we’ll take it just the way it is—light, open, and regardless of what those motors may be intended to power, likely very quick relative to whatever finished product it will eventually become. 

Neither we nor our spies have any idea exactly what these engineers are testing, but if it is indeed an early chassis mule, it’s likely for some sort of sports car. The layout allows for two passengers and not much more, and we can see the components of an air suspension fitted here, along with what appear to be aluminum upper and lower wishbones in the front suspension (along with a traditional anti-roll bar). 

Stefan Baldauf / SB-Medien 

While the mule’s proportions suggest a sports car, we shouldn’t jump to conclusions in that regard. It looks long and low, certainly, but it’s fitted with some awfully tall, skinny wheels and tires for a performance car. The rears appear to be some hard-worn Continentals with the branding scuffed off. 

Inside, there’s a full steering wheel (not necessarily a given these days) and some sport seats bolted to a wooden floor pan…
items.t: Be Brave: Mercedes Caught Testing a Death Kart That They Should Absolutely Sell

items.title: The Kia Telluride’s Only Fault Is Its Awful Climate Controls
items.summary:
The Kia Telluride is one of those vehicles that makes you wonder why people spend so much more money for the same basic product. It’s an extremely well-rounded big SUV that beats the competition soundly on value. But it’s not perfect. Both my colleague Joel Feder and I drove one in recent weeks, and came to the same conclusion: Kia’s climate-control touchscreen has got to go.

If you haven’t paid much attention to Kia design in recent years, the brand decided to stuff a tiny touch-sensitive display between the instrument cluster and central infotainment screen on its latest slate of models. This panel exclusively controls heating and air conditioning, which, on the surface, sounds great—here at  The Drive , we’re fans of more tiny screens with individual functions rather than bigger ones.

The problem is placement. Because of where this little display lives, it’s completely obscured by the right side of the steering wheel from a normal driving perspective. At least, it was for Joel and me. It’s no wonder this design choice annoyed us, because we’re both 5 feet, 10 inches tall.

Adam Ismail 

This quirk isn’t exclusive to the Telluride; the Kia K4 has it, as do the Seltos and EV3. I will admit, the first time I saw it on the K4, I thought it looked cool, but my fondness for it diminished with continued exposure in other vehicles. It’s one of those ideas that sounds good on paper and appears nice in a photo, until you encounter it in a practical setting. That’s when it becomes clear why automakers rarely put anything in that spot on the dash.

Fortunately, the Telluride does…
items.t: The Kia Telluride’s Only Fault Is Its Awful Climate Controls

items.title: This Jeep Wrangler With a Lamborghini Body Kit Is Like a Real-Life Hot Wheels Car
items.summary:
There’s nothing cooler than low-dollar, high-creativity car projects. And this lifted Jeep YJ, wearing a Lamborghini body kit made for a Pontiac Fiero , is one of the most creative things I’ve seen in a while! It’s the brainchild of Kyle Lewis, a gearhead in North Carolina who had an old Wrangler, stumbled on a neglected knockoff Countach, and turned them into this delightfully twisted caricature on wheels.

Lewis has posted quite a bit about the “Jeepborghini” on his Instagram page (the vehicle has its own IG and YouTube channel , too). “I was inspired to build this because I saw a Lamborghini body kit on a Pontiac Fiero parked at a parking lot for over 30 years. And I said, ‘I want it.’ So I bought it and started from there,” Lewis said.

What’s left of the Jeep is sitting on 35-inch tires. Since the vehicle’s so small, they look like they came off a monster truck. But perhaps the most impressive thing to me is that the scissor doors seem to be functioning properly. I’d imagine the fitment would be wobbly after decades of rotting in the sun, but I guess the kit car was made of tougher stuff than I’d have expected!

Lewis has some kind of speaker setup in the back, where a real Countach’s engine would be, completeing the video-game-character-car vibe quite nicely.

Kyle Lewis 

It’s really quite funny how well the Jeep and Pontiac wheelbases must have matched up, because it looks like the “Lambor”-body pretty much just dropped on top of the Wrangler chassis with the wheel wells in the right spots. The build took about four months. “Probably the most fun I had with this…
items.t: This Jeep Wrangler With a Lamborghini Body Kit Is Like a Real-Life Hot Wheels Car

items.title: How Tremec Figured Out a Manual Transmission for the C8 Corvette When GM Wouldn’t Do It
items.summary:
When Tremec told the world last year that it had developed a manual gearbox for the automatic-only C8 Chevrolet Corvette, the announcement created quite a stir. That buzz wasn’t limited to enthusiast chatter on social media; even Corvette Executive Chief Engineer Tony Roma commented on the existence (or lack thereof, at the time) of Tremec’s gearbox . Things got a bit tense, perhaps, and some were left with the impression that Tremec was dunking on GM for lacking the imagination necessary to make a manual C8 happen.

The real story, of course, is quite different. I touched on this in my brief drive of the first manual-swapped C8 by Peitz Performance , but here’s the longer version: GM’s decision had nothing to do with its engineering capabilities and everything to do with budgets. Roma has made no bones about it: a key component of the Corvette formula is affordability, and simply offering a second gearbox meant doubling the budget for an already whole-cloth transmission redesign.

“Transmissions are super expensive,” Roma told us on The Drivecast ( the full transcript is published here on the site ). “When we had C5, C6, and C7, we could use basically the same manual transmission architecture that had been around and slowly developed over like 30 years, and it was mostly paid for, and we were doing slight upgrades on it, and it cost reasonable amounts of money to keep it in production.”

Byron Hurd, Andrew P. Collins 

What happened? Like everything else in the C8 (save the V8 itself, really), its fundamental design had to be thrown out the window due to the car’s…
items.t: Here’s Why GM Never Built a Manual C8 Corvette—and Why Its Own Transmission Supplier Did

items.title: Turo’s Black Friday Deal: $50 Off Your Holiday Road Trip
items.summary:
Turo’s a fun way to rent cars you wouldn’t find at an airport counter. Plus, you get to pick a specific vehicle, rather than “whatever, or similar” that big rental brands give you. Turo’s peer-to-peer car rental setup is now running a holiday promo, and first-time American renters can use code TURO50TT to get $50 off a reservation of $250 or more.

The fine print: the code works from November 26 through December 8 at 11:59 p.m. ET, for trips taking place between November 28 and January 4. It’s limited to one use per guest, first-timers only, and capped at the first 4,000 redemptions. Additional terms apply.

There are definitely some cool and fun cars on Turo. You can rent yourself anything from a triple-black Land Rover Defender to a C8 Corvette to an FSD-equipped Tesla . With Turo Delivered, the car can also meet you at an airport, train station, hotel, or rental home, with no line or counter involved.

The peer-to-peer setup also means there’s a little more legwork—you’ve got to coordinate with someone from the internet, rather than just rolling up to a corporate desk. Pros and cons, right? But if you’re into cars or peer-to-peer programming in general, it’s a neat solution I’ve used a time or two myself.

Turo also sells digital gift cards for people who like to travel or are into cars on your holiday gift shopping list. Pick a design and an amount, then send it immediately or schedule it for later. Recipients redeem them on the app or Turo.com, and the credit never expires. Gift cards can only be bought and redeemed in the US.

items.title: Toyota Explains How It’s Trying to Fix Its Big Tundra Problem
items.summary:
Toyota, the world’s largest automaker, knows it has a problem: its Tundra truck engine is threatening its rock-solid reputation for reliability .

Now, the updated 2027 Toyota Tundra is arriving at dealerships and aims to address many issues with the current truck including but not limited to safety concerns with towing, infotainment limitations, ride quality issues, and more. Of course, Toyota’s angling for its change in machining processes for engine production to also hopefully fix its reliability issues. On the latest episode of The Drivecast , Toyota Tundra and Sequoia Assistant Chief Engineer Rob Crawford sat down exclusively with The Drive   to sort through the changes.

The Tundra ended up at the center of Toyota’s engine failure crisis . If you read The Drive or listen to this podcast, you know what I’m talking about. But for those who don’t, Toyota took a big swing when it introduced a 3.4 liter twin turbo V6 known as the V35A FTS in the current generation Tundra pickup and Sequoia SUV in 2022. It replaced the hardy 5.7 liter V8 used by those models for over a decade.

And at the time, a lot of people wondered if swapping a simple proven engine for a new high stress one would lead to problems. Sure enough, it did. The new V6 started destroying itself at notably high rates. As we’ve reported at length, including on this podcast back in June, the issue surrounds tiny bits of metal debris called swarf that get left behind in the engine block during manufacturing. Those shavings then adhere to the main bearing and cause knocking, rough idle, or total engine failure.…
items.t: Toyota Engineer Explains How It’s Fixing the Tundra
